failureModes.description: Failing agents repeatedly established brokenness or path safety before filesystem identity, so aliases and entries that were also shared lost the required shared-entry precedence.
failureModes.reasoning: This is not an unfair-test lead: the description explicitly says, "So are two entries whose recorded names resolve to one file, as when one links to that file" and "An entry both shared and something else stays shared." It is not best described as independent genuinely-hard failures because all nine implementations converged around the same ordering/identity assumption; artifacts repeatedly report outside-file sharers being discarded, linked targets being called unowned, or hard-link/index aliases escaping protection. Although the rule is subtle enough to miss, the cross-run convergence makes shared_blind_spot more informative than subtle_but_fair. For example, one log reports that the outside-file store became "{}" instead of retaining both alpha and beta entries, and the two-failure near-miss reports "unowned file: target" for an entry that recorded a link to that target.

output.reasoning: The working pool has a 1/10 legitimate pass rate, which is appropriate for an intentionally hard task. The sole passer completed both suites (its artifact says, "Agent passed all baseline and new tests with a legitimate implementation"), while every failing run still passed the baseline and reached functional assertions in the maintenance suite. Failures ranged from 2 to 33 of 136 new tests; the strongest near-miss artifact records "136 tests completed, 2 failed", while another records concrete path, hard-link, sharing, and unsafe-save failures. These are not a peripheral regression tripwire: they concern the requested integrity model itself, especially shared-entry precedence and filesystem identity. The one passing patch has about 800 effective production lines after excluding its added tests, documentation, imports/comments, so its median passing effort is comfortably above the 200-line thin-effort threshold; its production diff alone spans patch lines 1-1195 and expands the store by roughly 800 net lines. Message counts are also substantial (99-236). Searches of all artifacts found no reference implementation class names or locally surfaced prior solution, and the legitimate pass showed no test manipulation. Thus the runs corroborate a coherent, difficult, non-leaked task rather than exposing an agent-run discrepancy.
output.summary: Clean agent evidence: one substantial legitimate pass, nine substantive core-feature misses, no thin-solve, leakage, overlap, or false-positive signal.

output.reasoning:
The solution touches six files: four production Java files (`TextFileBasedViolationStore.java` and the three focused new helpers), one source documentation file, and the corresponding generated HTML guide. The HTML edit mirrors the AsciiDoc source and is consistent with `docs/build.gradle`, which renders the checked-in user guide into `docs/userguide/html`; there are no unrelated test, config, or production edits.

The required behavior traces cleanly through the patch. File-name configuration is isolated in the factory: `random` remains the non-deriving default, `description` produces deterministic ASCII-safe names bounded at 200 characters with an eligible whole-word fallback and a description fingerprint, and configured classes are instantiated only with a public no-argument constructor. Both initialization classification and saving reject null or empty strategy results when a name is actually requested, while `ignore` does not invoke a strategy merely to inspect entries. Constructor-supplied strategies use the same naming path and conflict with `default.fileNames` configuration as required.

Integrity mode parsing accepts only the three exact values. Index preconditions are checked before folder classification, including absent-index creation policy and direct regular-file identity. `StoreIntegrity` gives shared identity precedence (same recorded name, canonical/symbolic alias, or hard-link identity), then handles broken and resolved entries before derived-name collision, misplacement, and occupancy. It limits unowned findings to direct regular files, preserves line-break-only resolution semantics without changing ordinary carriage returns inside violations, and sorts reports by condition and rule/file key. Repair only writes the index after a successful discard or move; fail only reports. Save ownership is validated before inserting a new mapping, protects physical aliases of the index and external/unowned targets, and repair-mode empty saves safely forget known rules while preserving shared files and retaining the entry on deletion failure.

The existing per-canonical-index shared properties object now serializes saves with repair/fail examinations, so no integrity pass observes the index/file pair halfway through a save. The implementation follows package conventions and existing exception, reflection-annotation, line-normalization, and synchronization patterns. No visible Spotless/unused-import, SpotBugs, Java compatibility, generated-file-sync, API-stability, irrelevant-change, or AI-slop defect is present. Dynamic verification independently passed all 136 new tests and all 42 selected baseline tests, including maintained concurrency and save-permission regressions.
output.summary: Clean, substantive implementation of naming, integrity classification/repair/fail behavior, safe saves, and in-process coordination; documentation and generated output are synchronized and no solution defect is evident.

output.authorGuidance:
Strengthen the suite before resubmitting. In the mixed fail-report test, choose rule and file names whose lexical order conflicts with the required broken/resolved/shared/unowned group order, so a globally sorted report fails. In the rejected null/empty-name save test, snapshot or reload `stored.rules` and assert that no mapping was added. Also add a custom naming strategy case with a CRLF-bearing rule description to preserve the public strategy input contract.

The agent runs show that this is a genuinely hard task, not a broken one. Most implementations made the same mistake: they classified broken or unsafe paths before determining whether entries shared the same underlying file. The description already states that shared status wins, so this convergence reflects subtle filesystem reasoning rather than a missing clarification.

Keep the fail-safe test harness, the broad path/link/hard-link and concurrency coverage, and the focused reference implementation. The implementation passed both the full maintenance suite and the selected baseline suite, and its ownership checks, condition ordering, and synchronization structure are solid.

The broad suite is deterministic and exercises the requested behavior, but two verified High coverage holes admit realistic wrong implementations. First, the only mixed-condition ordering assertion uses representative names already in the required lexical order, so globally sorting all findings would pass. The strongest disproof—that another test checks cross-condition ordering—fails: the remaining order tests cover only ordering within individual conditions. Second, the rejected empty-name save path never inspects stored.rules, so an implementation can persist an empty mapping before throwing. The strongest disproof—that another assertion observes this exact ignore-then-save state—also fails; index snapshots appear in companion initialization and other safety paths, not this path. A Medium gap also leaves the public custom-strategy CRLF input behavior uncovered. High is therefore the most severe kept tests issue, yielding band 1.

I found no path that succeeds with non-JUnit output at --output_path and no platform-content leak. Dynamic checks confirm the 42 selected baseline tests pass, all 136 new tests fail on base and pass with the reference, and six repeated runs were stable. The hidden suite is unusually broad and its assertions are fair. However, two concrete T3 holes still admit realistic nonconforming implementations: the mixed report-order fixture accidentally uses tokens already ordered lexicographically, and the no-name save test does not inspect stored.rules after rejection. A further public-extension edge involving CRLF-bearing rule descriptions is not covered. The High findings determine band 1.
